items.title: Performance of Naïve Spectral Geometric Models in Histopathology AI
items.abstract: Abstract Spectral geometric methods provide mathematically interpretable representations of tissue morphology, yet their standalone performance in histopathology artificial intelligence has not been systematically evaluated. This study benchmarks purely spectral pipelines across representative digital pathology and spatial omics tasks relative to convolutional baselines. Spectral features derived from graph Laplacians, heat kernel signatures, spectral wavelet energy, Slepian concentrations, fractal descriptors, and persistent homology were extracted from histopathology patches using fixed-grid graphs. Features were processed using spectral neural operators and gradient boosting. Four tasks were evaluated: binary breast cancer classification (BreaKHis), multi-class glioblastoma region-patch classification, spatial transcriptomics prediction (10× Visium), and spot-wise denoising. Cross-validation and leave-one-slide-out strategies were applied. Metrics included accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), mean squared error, and Pearson correlation. Equivalence between spectral and CNN models was not established within the prespecified ±0.03 AUC margin. Purely spectral models achieved lower performance than convolutional baselines, with AUC differences of 0.12–0.23. The CNN→LGBM model achieved an accuracy of 0.83 ± 0.06, balanced accuracy of 0.73 ± 0.10, and AUC of 0.80 ± 0.13. Equivalence was not established within the prespecified margin. Fusion achieved balanced accuracy of 0.73 ± 0.08, equal to the CNN baseline mean balanced accuracy, without surpassing CNN AUC. Spatial transcriptomics prediction showed limited cross-slide generalization (Pearson correlation 0.06), whereas spot-wise denoising under sparse conditions showed competitive performance. Spectral geometric models do not outperform convolutional methods for classification or segmentation but provide complementary utility in denoising and sparse spatial settings.

items.title: Physical and Mental Health Consequences of Work-Related Stress: A Comparative Study of Women and Men
items.abstract: Work-related stress is a leading occupational health concern, and a substantial literature suggests its consequences differ between women and men. Most of that literature, however, establishes that a difference exists without identifying the mechanism responsible. This study examined the physical and mental health consequences of work-related stress among employed women and men, and tested whether differences persisted after psychosocial working conditions were controlled. A comparative cross-sectional design was adopted. Data were collected from 101 full-time employees aged 25-50 in Bengaluru, India; the analytical sample comprised 100 participants (50 women, 50 men). A 50-item instrument assessed perceived stress, working conditions, physical symptoms, emotional wellbeing and coping. Physical health and emotional wellbeing scales showed good reliability (alpha = .83 and .86). Five of six hypotheses were unsupported: women and men did not differ in perceived stress (p = .584, d = -0.11), physical symptoms (p = .986, d = 0.004) or emotional wellbeing (p = .575, d = 0.11), and gender did not moderate the stress-health relationship. One significant difference emerged: men reported greater problem-focused coping (p < .001, d = -0.73), although the predicted difference in emotion-focused coping did not appear. Perceived stress correlated strongly with physical symptoms (r = .55) and emotional wellbeing (r = .62), explaining 30% and 39% of variance. Findings are consistent with a differential-exposure account: where working conditions were comparable, health consequences were comparable.

items.title: PIU Smart Intelligence Agents: Design and Implementation of a Security-Aware Multi-Agent Architecture for Enterprise Intelligence
items.abstract: Enterprises increasingly rely on heterogeneous documents, relational databases, and analytical systems to support information retrieval and business decision-making. Integrating large language models (LLMs) with these sources introduces challenges in evidence reliability, analytical correctness, access control, and operational resilience. This paper presents PIU Smart Intelligence Agents, a security-aware multi-agent architecture designed to integrate enterprise document intelligence, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), semantic search, document summarization, naturallanguage-to-SQL analytics, key performance indicator (KPI) generation, and conversational AI within a common application and governance framework. The proposed architecture organizes specialized AI capabilities around shared services for authentication, authorization, request validation, provider integration, observability, and controlled data access. Its document-processing workflow encompasses file validation, text extraction, optical character recognition for scanned documents, normalization, chunking, embedding generation, and vector-based indexing. The structured-analytics workflow separates schema-aware query generation from SQL validation, restricted database execution, and result interpretation. The architecture also addresses provider compatibility, timeout handling, failure recovery, document lifecycle management, and traceability of generated outputs. The source implementation reports 1,242 automated tests passed and two integration tests skipped. These results are reported implementation evidence and have not been independently reproduced. The available evidence does not establish comprehensive external RAG benchmark performance, quantitative correctness across all agents, independently validated security effectiveness, or production-scale performance and recovery guarantees. Accordingly, this study presents an integrated engineering architecture and identifies a reproducible evaluation framework for assessing its effectiveness. The principal contribution is the systematic integration of heterogeneous enterprise AI capabilities with explicit governance and validation requirements, rather than the introduction of a new learning or retrieval algorithm. Future work should prioritize agent-specific correctness testing, retrieval and answer-quality benchmarks, adversarial security evaluation, controlled load testing, and recovery verification.

items.title: Pixels to precision: Deep learning in dental imaging
items.abstract: Dental imaging is fundamental to diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up in Oral Medicine and Maxillofacial Radiology. Although conventional radiographic interpretation remains dependent on professional expertise, diagnostic performance may be influenced by observer variability, image quality, workload, and the subtle nature of early pathological changes. The development of Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL), has introduced new approaches for automated analysis of dental and maxillofacial images. This narrative review discusses the evolution, principles, applications, clinical relevance, limitations, and future directions of deep learning in dental imaging, with emphasis on intraoral radiography, panoramic radiography, cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), and related imaging modalities. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated applications in dental caries detection, periodontal bone assessment, periapical lesion detection, tooth identification and numbering, jaw lesion analysis, anatomical segmentation, and treatment planning. More advanced architectures, including U-Net, residual networks, object-detection models, three-dimensional CNNs, and emerging transformer-based systems, have expanded the scope of automated image interpretation. However, the rapid growth of research has also highlighted important limitations, including small and heterogeneous datasets, inconsistent annotation, retrospective study designs, limited external validation, algorithmic bias, and difficulties in explaining model predictions. Importantly, high algorithmic accuracy does not necessarily translate into clinical effectiveness. Future research should therefore focus on diverse multicentre datasets, external and prospective validation, explainable AI, multimodal systems, ethical governance, and meaningful human-AI collaboration. Deep learning is most appropriately viewed as an adjunctive clinical decision-support technology that complements rather than replaces professional diagnostic judgment.

items.title: PlaceIntel: A Multi-Agentic AI-Powered Campus Placement Management and Preparation Platform
items.abstract: Abstract— Preparing students for campus recruitment in a personalized and effective way is still difficult for most colleges. Typical placement systems deal mainly with administrative work such as registering students, storing company details, checking eligibility, and organizing recruitment drives, whereas interview training and companyspecific preparation are usually left to separate resources. This paper describes PlaceIntel, a web platform driven by multiple cooperating AI agents that unites central placement administration with tailored AI support for students. Four dedicated agents form the core of the system: a Mock Interview Agent, a Company Preparation Agent, a Company Research Agent, and a Skill Gap Analyzer. A Candidate Evaluation module additionally supports structured assessment during placement drives. The implementation relies on React, Java Spring Boot, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Redis, LangGraph, and Gemini 3.6 Flash; authentication is handled with Spring Security and JWT, while Docker and AWS are used for deployment. The resulting architecture brings placement operations and AI-guided preparationtogether within a single modular design.

items.title: PointerBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Fine-Grained GUI Grounding
items.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models have shown promising performance in computer-use tasks, from planning user workflows to grounding natural-language actions to precise UI targets. Existing end-to-end benchmarks primarily emphasize long-horizon task completion, while GUI grounding benchmarks remain focused on conventional controls and a limited set of professional interfaces. We introduce POINTERBENCH, a diagnostic suite of 1,500 screenshot-instruction pairs probing three complementary capabilities: thin sub-element identification and geometric grounding in spreadsheets (POINTERBENCH-Sheets), character-level grounding in long-text documents (POINTERBENCH-Text), and mixed GUI grounding across 100 professional applications (POINTERBENCH-Pro). We carefully curate each task with pixel-exact target geometry and evaluate both general-purpose multimodal models and 39 specialist GUI grounding configurations. We find text grounding to be the most challenging setting, with Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and the leading native specialist UI-Venus-2-9B achieving 69.6%, 53.4%, and 25.8% success on POINTERBENCH-Text despite respective 83.2%, 77.7%, and 54.5% average success across POINTERBENCH. These results reveal substantial headroom in fine-grained GUI grounding across frontier and specialist models. We publicly release the benchmark and evaluation code at https://github.com/warmwindOS/pointerbench.

items.title: Pondus: an agentic structural analysis and design program built on the Stabileo engine
items.abstract: Language-model agents can now operate engineering programs through tool interfaces, but a structuralprogram that an agent drives has to be designed for that user, because the agent accepts whatever numbersthe tools return. This paper describes Pondus, an open-source native program in which a language-modelagent and an engineer work on one three-dimensional structural model, and reports how it is built, howit is used and how far its results can be trusted. The agent reaches the program through a Model ContextProtocol server of 44 tools, either from the chat panel of the desktop application, where a vendored agentharness runs one agent session per message on a copy of the model, or from external agents such asClaude Desktop and ChatGPT. Every tool calls the same functions as the engineer’s interface, so a modelbuilt by the agent can be checked, edited and undone by hand. The analysis runs on the Stabileo engine,which Pondus links as a library with four marked changes: Pondus splits members, transfers slab loads,generates shear walls as wide columns with rigid arms and builds the seismic mass before handing asolver input to the engine, and it designs to ACI 318-19, AISC 360-16 and EN 1993-1-1 from the results.Two agent runs with a low-cost model built, analysed and designed a two-storey frame in 105 s with 13tool calls and a five-storey frame with shear walls under an ASCE 7-22 response spectrum, including a16-page calculation report, in 382 s with 22 tool calls. Every number in the agent’s answers matched thetools and hand checks of the loads, the seismic weight and the base shear, but the answers also containedfour descriptive errors, such as reporting two deepened beams where the program had deepened six, andthey did not point out that the walls resist load only in one direction, so the response modification factorof the walls was applied to the frame direction as well. A calibration against 470 published, closed-formand independent reference values over 229 cases found 430 within 0.5 % and 449 within 1 %, and it foundfourteen defects, thirteen of them in the code that prepares the inputs of the engine and the design checksrather than in the numerical kernels. Together these results suggest that the tools of an agentic structuralprogram can be made accurate, whereas the agent’s prose remains the weaker link that the engineer mustread against the program’s own tables.

items.title: Potential Future Shifts in Television Production in Light of Technological Development
items.abstract: This research aims to anticipate potential future transformations in the television production industry amidst rapid technological advancements and to examine their impact on production quality and the efficiency of technical and professional processes. It also seeks to identify the key challenges media organizations face in adopting and integrating modern technologies into television production environments. The study focuses on three main areas: the role of modern technologies in enhancing television production quality; the technical, human, economic, and organizational challenges associated with their adoption; and the impact of artificial intelligence applications—a prominent feature of contemporary technological transformation—on production process efficiency. The study employed a descriptive methodology, utilizing a questionnaire to gather data from a sample of 400 participants—professionals and staff within the radio and television sectors. The sample encompassed broadcasters, directors, editors, producers, engineers, technicians, media researchers, and marketing and advertising personnel, as well as channel and station managers and consultants in technology and IT. This approach enabled an examination of diverse professional perspectives regarding the current state of technological transformations and their potential future trends. The research findings indicate that modern technological advancements—particularly artificial intelligence applications—play a significant role in evolving television production processes. This is achieved by enhancing audio and visual quality, developing visual effects, improving content management efficiency, automating certain operational tasks, and minimizing human error. Conversely, the results reveal a number of challenges that could hinder the adoption of these technologies, most notably high costs and the need to upgrade the professional and technical skills of the workforce. In light of these findings, the research discusses potential future transformations in the television production industry—specifically the shift toward smarter, more flexible production environments, the reshaping of certain professional roles, and the increasing reliance on advanced technical solutions across various stages of production.

items.title: Precision Cardiovascular Medicine: Integrating Pharmacogenomics, Biomarkers, Artificial Intelligence, and Real-World Evidence
items.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains a major global cause of morbidity and mortality, with substantial interindividual variation in disease risk, treatment response, and susceptibility to adverse effects. Precision cardiovascular medicine incorporates patient-level information to refine cardiovascular prevention, diagnosis, risk stratification, and treatment. This structured narrative review is based on a structured literature search, with 213 publications included in the synthesis. This review synthesizes evidence on four complementary domains: pharmacogenomics, biomarkers, artificial intelligence (AI), and real-world evidence (RWE), and examines their potential integration in cardiovascular care. Pharmacogenomics has established applications in selected gene–drug pairs, including CYP2C19–clopidogrel, CYP2C9/VKORC1–warfarin, and SLCO1B1–statin-associated muscle toxicity, although implementation varies according to evidence, accessibility, and clinical infrastructure. Biomarker research extends beyond cardiac troponins to markers of myocardial stress, fibrosis, inflammation, and molecular regulation, including soluble ST2, galectin-3, GDF-15, and microRNAs. AI and machine learning provide approaches for analyzing multimodal cardiovascular data and have been investigated for risk assessment, phenotyping, imaging, ECG analysis, and clinical decision support. RWE complements randomized evidence by providing information on treatment utilization, safety, effectiveness, and outcomes in routine-care populations, while challenges include data quality, confounding, and incomplete ascertainment. Across coronary artery disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and inherited cardiovascular diseases, increasing opportunities exist to integrate these domains. However, clinical translation remains influenced by validation, interpretability, generalizability, cost, regulation, data governance, and health equity. Future research should emphasize prospective evaluation, diverse-population validation, interoperable infrastructure, and assessment of clinical utility to support the responsible integration of precision approaches into cardiovascular care.

items.title: Predicting acute intracranial vascular events in stroke alerts using large-language models and structured data
items.abstract: Acute stroke alerts are frequently activated for non-cerebrovascular conditions, creating false positives that strain resources and increase diagnostic uncertainty. We developed machine learning models integrating large-language models, structured electronic health record data, and clinical time-series features to predict acute intracranial vascular event (AIVE) at stroke alert activation. Using retrospective stroke alerts from the Mount Sinai Health System (2011–2021), we extracted demographics, comorbidities, medications, vital signs, laboratory results, and clinical notes documented before alert activation. AIVE was defined using radiographic gold standards as a composite of acute cerebrovascular and selected acute intracranial diagnoses. Notes were modeled using Clinical-Longformer, MxBAI embeddings with a feed-forward neural network, and BioWordVec embeddings with logistic regression; structured-data models used complementary hyperparameter-tuned workflows. Model outputs were combined in a late-fusion stacked ensemble and evaluated on internal and within-system held-out hospital test sets. Among 16,512 stroke alerts, 9,013 (55.6%) were due to AIVE. The multimodal model achieved an AUROC of 0.73 (95% CI, 0.71–0.75), positive predictive value of 0.68, sensitivity of 0.76, F1-score of 0.72, and specificity of 0.56 on internal testing, with similar held-out hospital performance. This approach may support post-activation stroke-alert risk stratification and reduce false-positive evaluations.

items.title: Predicting Music Valence and Arousal via Textual and Multimodal In-Context Learning in Large Language Models
items.abstract: While arousal can be reliably predicted from musical audio, emotional valence remains difficult to model due to its subjective and context-dependent nature. In this work, we investigate the potential of in-context learning (ICL) with large language models to advance continuous valence and arousal prediction. Rather than predicting emotion scores directly, our framework leverages contextual demonstrations from an auxiliary dataset to refine the initial predictions produced by a small, task-specific base model. We systematically evaluate a text-based ICL variant using lyrics and generated audio captions, alongside a multimodal variant that incorporates raw audio signals. Using the entire MER60 dataset strictly as a held-out test set, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains, particularly for valence. Text-based ICL improves the valence $R^2$ from 0.110 to 0.427 with 80 demonstration shots, while the multimodal variant achieves 0.346 with only 10 shots. These findings suggest that training-free ICL offers an effective inference-time strategy for current language models to predict continuous music emotion.

items.title: Predictive Analytics for Supply Chain Resilience and Logistics Optimisation in Volatile Operating Environments
items.abstract: Introduction: Volatile operating environments create demand uncertainty, supplier disruptions, delivery delays, geopolitical shocks, and other events that can negatively affect operational performance and supply chain resilience. Evidence on the contribution of predictive analytics to both logistics optimisation and resilience is still fragmented, and opportunities exist to anticipate these risks and inform timely logistics decision-making. This systematic review aims to collate evidence on the use of predictive analytics to improve supply chain resilience and optimise logistics operations in volatile operating environments, with a specific focus on predictive techniques, applications, outcomes, and implementation challenges. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020. Terms relating to predictive analytics, supply chains and logistics, resilience and risk, and optimisation were used to search Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection. Eligible studies applied machine learning, deep learning, artificial intelligence (AI)-based predictive modelling, or related forecasting approaches to problems involving uncertainty, disruption, risk, resilience, or optimisation in supply-chain and/or logistics settings. After deduplication, 321 unique records were screened by title and abstract; 30 reports underwent full-text assessment, and 15 studies were included in the synthesis. Results: The 15 included studies showed substantial methodological and contextual heterogeneity. Applications concentrated on demand forecasting, inventory management, supplier risk, disruption prediction, and product availability. Methods included ensemble learning, deep learning, hybrid models, and adaptive approaches. Predictive performance often improved relative to study-specific comparators, although greater model complexity did not consistently produce better performance. The clearest operational gains were reported when predictions were coupled with optimisation or decision-support processes such as inventory allocation, replenishment, and supplier selection. Evidence relevant to resilience was strongest for anticipation, visibility, response, and recovery, whereas direct evidence for longer-term adaptation remained limited. Common implementation constraints included data quality, data availability, model adaptability, interpretability, and organisational infrastructure. Conclusion: Predictive analytics can support supply-chain resilience and logistics performance when predictive outputs are translated into timely operational decisions. The evidence remains heterogeneous and context-dependent; future research should prioritise external validation, longitudinal assessment, and direct measurement of resilience outcomes.

items.title: Predictive Underground Water Leakage Detection Using Artificial Intelligence and the Internet of Things
items.abstract: Unaccounted-for water loss resulting from undetected underground pipe leaks poses a persistent operational and financial challenge for municipal distribution systems worldwide. In conventional utility practice, leaks are predominantly identified reactively—either when water eventually breaches the surface or following localized pressure drop complaints from consumers. In this paper, we develop a proactive, multi-sensor predictive leakage detection framework that pairs a low-power edge Internet of Things (IoT) architecture with a hybrid machine learning pipeline. Subsurface pipe segments are monitored using five complementary sensing modalities: hydraulic pressure, inline flow velocity, pipe-wall structural vibration via a MEMS accelerometer, soil moisture, and ambient temperature. Sensor readings are acquired, pre-filtered, and transmitted by an energy-efficient ESP32-based edge node using LoRa wireless communication and TLS-secured MQTT to a central analytics backend. A sliding-window feature extraction stage derives short-term statistical trends and feeds an unsupervised Isolation Forest model; the resulting anomaly metric is concatenated with temporal features to train a gradient boosting classifier that forecasts the likelihood of a leak initiating within a two-hour predictive lead window (H = 12 steps). We evaluate the proposed approach on a synthetic distribution network of 60 pipe segments that explicitly incorporates gradual, incipient mechanical degradation prior to burst onset. Benchmarked against a conventional static pressure threshold (F1 = 0.830) and standard supervised classifiers, the proposed hybrid model achieves an F1-score of 0.992 and provides a median warning lead time of 1.9 hours (mean 1.8 hours) ahead of physical rupture, with zero false alarms and zero missed events across held-out test segments. Finally, we analyze model sensitivity across noise regimes and establish key deployment requirements for district metered area field implementations.

items.title: Present, Yet Unseen: Investigating OSF Search Omissions, Recovery, and Institutional Connections
items.abstract: Public research depends on being discoverable. This investigation documents a failure in that basic function: two public OSF registrations—The Irreversible Constraint Regime and The Life Equation—were accessible through their direct records but absent from the registration-search results tested. The preserved evidence records a concrete discrepancy. The public contributor API listed 21 registrations, while the corresponding search returned 19, omitting these two works. Their records identified them as public, accepted, unembargoed, and not withdrawn. Stored metadata cards contained their titles, identifiers, and authorship, yet the documented searches failed to retrieve them. The investigation preserves screenshots, exact API responses, timestamps, correspondence, and cryptographic integrity hashes so that these observations can be independently examined. Following the author’s inquiry, discoverability was restored. OSF Support confirmed a manual SHARE re-index and subsequently stated that it had re-indexed the public content at the author’s request. In its October 22, 2026 response, OSF described the original problem as an “indexing error, of which there is no known cause.” It also stated that indexing history and content-indexing logs are not retained, and that no AdminLogEntry records are created for indexing. Those statements make the limits of the available explanation central to this investigation. Restored search results establish recovery; they do not establish when the omissions began, why these records were affected, or whether the underlying condition could recur. The dossier compares OSF’s account with the preserved metadata-refresh sequence, examines seven outside projects that also refreshed during the observed window, and records ICR’s zero-byte storage-metadata discrepancy. A separate relationship appendix documents professional contacts and institutional connections involving OSF and the Center for Open Science, CERN and Zenodo, university research groups, and technology companies. It includes Leonardo Auri and Yaroslav Halchenko, who reported distinct technical problems. Every connection is identified by its actual relationship: public software exchange, governance role, institutional affiliation, shared release credit, hosting, or disclosed support. These records provide context without establishing either reporter’s responsibility for the omissions. The project’s purpose is to preserve an auditable account of what failed, what changed, what OSF acknowledged, and what remains unresolved about the reliability and traceability of public research discovery. _______________________________________________________ Update — October 22, 2026: The follow-up questions refer to Blaine’s initial response and should be read alongside OSF Support’s subsequent partial answers. OSF stated that it manually re-indexed the public content at the author’s request, reported completion at 2:00 p.m. EDT on October 21, and described the original omission as an indexing error with “no known cause.” It also stated that indexing history, content-indexing logs, and indexing AdminLogEntry records are not retained or created. These replies clarify the recovery procedure but leave the original cause, onset, responsible operator, and full scope unresolved. The October 22 replies identify their sender as OSF Support, without naming an individual author. The investigation remains open to further clarification and supporting records. Investigation performed by Dustin Sprenger, my emergent artificial intelligence ABEL, and OpenAI GPT.

items.title: Prevalence and functional impact of musculoskeletal pain among university students in seven Arab countries and its sociodemographic and lifestyle associations
items.abstract: Musculoskeletal pain (MSP) represents a major public health challenge globally, particularly among university students who are in a critical transitional phase of life characterized by intense academic demands, lifestyle changes, and increasing reliance on digital technologies. Sedentary behavior (SB) has been identified as a potential risk factor for MSP; however, evidence from the Arab region remains limited. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of MSP in nine body regions (neck, shoulders, upper back, elbows, wrists/hands, lower back, hips/thighs, knees, and ankles/feet) across four time points (lifetime, past 12 months, past month, and today), to assess the impact of MSP, and examine the association between SB and MSP. A multinational cross-sectional study was conducted among 4300 university students in seven Arab countries (Egypt, Yemen, Iraq, Sudan, Jordan, Syria, and Palestine), using an online Arabic self-administered questionnaire. Convenience and snowball sampling methods were used to recruit eligible study respondents. MSP was assessed using the Arabic version of the Extended Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (NMQ-E). SB was assessed using sedentary behavior questionnaire (SBQ). Chi-square tests were used for univariate associations. Binary logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with any MSP in the past 12 months, and to identify predictors of high SB. Adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were reported, and a p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The prevalence of MSP in at least one body region was 84.0% (lifetime), 71.3% (past 12 months), and 64.9% (past month). The neck (49.3%) and lower back (37.3%) were the most affected regions in the past 12 months. Among those affected, preventing usual activities (range: 48.8%–71.7%) and taking medication (range: 37.6–48.2%) were the most reported impacts, while hospitalization remained relatively low (3.2–14.2%). Female sex (aOR = 1.98, 95% CI 1.69–2.31), chronic diseases (aOR = 1.90, 95% CI 1.44–2.49), MSP family history (aOR = 1.96, 95% CI 1.56–2.47), moderate SB (aOR = 1.56, 95% CI 1.32–1.84), and high SB (aOR = 1.42, 95% CI 1.16–1.72) were significantly associated with MSP in the past 12 months, while sleeping 6–8 h was protective (aOR = 0.79, 95% CI 0.67–0.92). This study found a high prevalence of MSP among university students in Arab countries, particularly affecting the neck and lower back. Higher SB, chronic diseases, and a family history of MSP were associated with MSP, whereas adequate sleep appeared to be protective. These findings support the need for university-based strategies that reduce prolonged SB and promote musculoskeletal health, including ergonomic education, active breaks, adjustable study stations, and more active learning environments.

items.title: Prevalence of and factors associated with low back pain among construction workers in Mogadishu, Somalia
items.abstract: Background Low back pain (LBP) is a leading cause of disability, particularly in labor-intensive industries. While biomechanical hazards are well-documented in developed nations, epidemiological data from unregulated construction sectors in post-conflict regions remains extremely scarce. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence and identify factors associated with LBP among manual construction workers in Mogadishu, Somalia. Methods An analytic cross-sectional study was conducted among 191 manual workers recruited via stratified random sampling from five major construction companies. Data were collected using a culturally-adapted Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire to assess socio-demographic, lifestyle, and occupational exposures. We utilized a multivariable mixed-effects logistic regression model, accounting for clustering by company, to identify independent associated factors. Results are reported as adjusted odds ratios (AOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results The workforce was notably young (median age = 26 years), registering an LBP period prevalence of 51.9% (95% CI: 43.5–60.3%). In the adjusted analysis, income status was the strongest predictor, with workers living below extreme poverty facing elevated odds of LBP (AOR = 7.60; 95% CI: 2.48–23.28). Other factors significantly associated included possessing over six years of work experience (AOR = 4.85; 95% CI: 1.56–15.11), being underweight (AOR = 5.22; 95% CI: 1.24–21.94), tobacco use (AOR = 5.70; 95% CI: 1.94–16.78), and inadequate sleep duration of fewer than six hours (AOR = 4.11; 95% CI: 1.28–13.24). Biomechanically, frequency of heavy lifting (AOR = 4.29; 95% CI: 1.26–14.56) and bending (AOR = 5.35; 95% CI: 1.33–21.45) were strongly associated with reporting LBP. Conclusion LBP is highly prevalent among construction workers in Mogadishu. The factors associated with LBP were extreme poverty, inadequate physiological tissue recovery, and severe biomechanical overload. Mitigating this crisis requires site-level ergonomic interventions, such as team-lifting protocols, alongside overarching policies that establish baseline wages to address foundational socioeconomic hazards.

items.title: Privacy Concerns, Perceived Privacy Control, and Trust in Google Digital Services: Evidence on Continued Use Intention among Young Users in Bangladesh
items.abstract: The expansion of Google digital services and the growing integration of generative artificial intelligence have intensified the importance of privacy, user control, and trust in digital-service relationships. This study examines whether privacy concern and perceived privacy control are associated with trust in Google digital services and whether these perceptions, together with trust, explain users’ intention to continue using Google/Gemini services in Bangladesh. Drawing on Privacy Calculus Theory and Trust Theory, the study develops a model in which privacy concern is expected to reduce trust, perceived privacy control is expected to strengthen trust, and trust is expected to increase continued-use intention. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey design was applied to the Group 2 Google master dataset. After screening, 385 complete cases were retained, with all retained respondents satisfying the attention-check criterion. Three-item measures captured privacy concern, perceived privacy control, trust, and continued-use intention using a five-point Likert scale. Composite-score regressions with bootstrap inference were used to reproduce the planned SEM/PLSSEM-oriented structural assessment. The results indicate that perceived privacy control positively predicts trust (β = .167, p = .001), whereas privacy concern does not have a statistically significant effect on trust (β = .080, p = .114). Trust is a substantial positive predictor of continued-use intention (β = .347, p < .001), and perceived privacy control also has a positive direct association with continued use (β = .129, p = .007). Privacy concern does not significantly predict continued use (β = .058, p = .217). Bootstrap mediation indicates a significant indirect effect of perceived privacy control through trust, while the privacy-concern indirect effect is not statistically distinguishable from zero. The findings suggest that users’ perceived ability to understand and manage privacy settings may be more consequential for trust and continued use than generalized privacy concern alone. The study contributes Bangladesh-specific evidence to privacy-calculus and trust research and offers practical implications for Google and other digital-service providers seeking to strengthen transparency, user control, and durable trust in the generative-AI era.

items.title: Professional perspectives on sensory and spatial barriers relevant to neuro-inclusive secondary school environments in Nigeria
items.abstract: Introduction Sensory and spatial characteristics of learning environments can influence how neurodivergent students participate in education. This study examined professional accounts of built‐environment barriers relevant to neuro-inclusive secondary‐school design in Nigeria. Methods Seven multidisciplinary professionals were interviewed virtually using a semi‐structured guide. Four had direct experience with secondary‐school‐aged learners, while others worked in therapeutic, special‐needs, rehabilitation, or care/support settings. Open‐ended responses were analysed inductively using reflexive thematic analysis, while responses to nine predefined design features were synthesised separately as prompted feature appraisals. Results Four themes were generated: sensory environmental stressors; environmental distress and spatial dysregulation; restorative and regulatory features; and spatial configuration, transition, and classroom ergonomics. Auditory and visual conditions, crowding, abrupt transitions, and limited retreat space were prominent concerns. Funding, space, institutional readiness, and implementation knowledge affected feasibility. A preliminary three‐tier retrofit framework prioritised acoustic control, lighting control, withdrawal/escape spaces, and sensory zoning (Tier 1); flexible furniture and wayfinding/predictability (Tier 2); and biophilic respite, visual simplification/colour, and temperature/ventilation (Tier 3). Discussion The findings provide mixed‐context professional proxy evidence relevant to Nigerian secondary‐school design. The framework is preliminary and unvalidated and should be tested through co‐design with neurodivergent students and objective environmental assessment.

items.title: Progress Probes $P^2$: Lightweight Runtime Monitoring for Vision-Language-Action Models
items.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform diverse manipulation tasks directly from visual observations and natural language instructions, but they remain prone to mistakes and unpredictable failures. Deploying these policies without continuous human supervision will require robust runtime monitors that detect when the policy has gone off-course. Existing monitors use external foundation models, such as vision-language models (VLMs) to supervise the policy, introducing significant complexity and computational cost for monitoring at runtime. In this work, we investigate an alternate approach: \textit{can a VLA's own internal activations provide the information needed to monitor its execution?} Our method trains linear probes on policy activations from demonstrations to estimate progress, then flags executions that deviate from expected progress. In experiments with the open-source VLA $π_{0.5}$ and across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, this approach is competitive with or outperforms VLM-based monitors in task failure detection, as well as methods which require failure data for training. These findings suggest that simple probes of VLA internals can be used to develop reliable runtime monitors, opening a path toward building policies that can act reliably and monitor their execution without external foundation models.

items.title: Prompting Strategy Effects Depend on the Judge: A Multilingual Study of LLM-as-a-Judge Robustness
items.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation is increasingly applied to multilingual tasks, yet prompting strategies such as Chain-of-Thought and Role Conditioning are recommended based solely on English benchmarks. Whether their effectiveness transfers across judge models and languages remains unknown: prompt-sensitivity studies are largely English-centric, while existing multilingual judge studies fix the prompt template. In this work, we address this gap by measuring this interaction through a benchmark of 9 prompting strategies, 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages, and 4 tasks across 13 datasets, yielding over 1M pointwise scores on gold-reference outputs, validated against human judgments. We find that prompting strategies are not transferable: the choice of the judge model dominates the choice of prompting strategy, strategy effects reverse direction across judges, and stability degrades in low-resource languages, where these effects are concealed by aggregate reporting. These findings show that prompting effects in multilingual evaluation are conditioned on the judge, task, and language. Consequently, prompting strategies should be validated for the intended evaluation setting, and cross-study comparisons should account for both judge and prompt configuration.

items.title: ProtocolNerd: An Interactive AI Research Assistant for Scientific Protocol Discovery
items.abstract: A search for a suitable experimental protocol using keywords may not lead to the most appropriate protocol, because the keywords may not include exactly the right terms. ProtocolNerd is a web-based interactive assistant that helps biologists and chemists (so far) find relevant protocols by describing their experiment in plain English and then answering a few follow-up questions. Through these domain-specific questions, users optionally provide additional details about the experiment, such as the organism, sample type, technique, and experimental readout. The system uses these answers to build a profile describing the experiment. For biologists, the system then (i) searches Protocols.io for relevant protocols using TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency) keyword matching and embedding-based semantic search, and (ii) queries PubMed with a reformulated version of the request to retrieve related research papers. For chemists, the system searches Europe PMC and PubMed. ProtocolNerd ranks the retrieved protocols and papers based on how well they match the researcher’s intent and explains why each result may be relevant. We have evaluated ProtocolNerd on molecular biology queries with a citation-grounded benchmark of 100 papers, each of which cites a particular protocol in its Methods section. Using a short automatically (large language model)-generated query on each such paper’s abstract, ProtocolNerd placed the confirmed protocol within its top 10 results 46% of the time. A non-parametric paired test shows that this was significantly better than two strong baselines. On the same benchmark it also found the protocol significantly more often than three general AI research assistants, Elicit (20%), Consensus (8%), and Perplexity (5%). These results suggest that combining interactive profiling, multiple retrieval methods, re-ranking, and explainability can significantly improve protocol discovery for scientific research. When applied to chemistry, ProtocolNerd found 31% of the protocols (or their equivalents) using Europe PMC alone and 45% when including PubMed.

items.title: Psychological Well-being in Sports Coaching: Determinants, Dynamics and Practical Implications
items.abstract: Psychological well-being at work has become a central topic in organizational and sport psychology because it bears on health, performance, and the sustainability of a career. Sports coaches work under heavy demands: large workloads, competitive pressure, and complex interpersonal relationships. Such conditions can affect their well-being, which in turn shapes how they coach, the decisions they make, and the outcomes they achieve. This chapter sets out the conceptual foundations of psychological well-being and considers their relevance to the coaching profession. It reviews the main theoretical models, including hedonic and eudaimonic approaches, and examines how job demands are balanced against personal resources, drawing on positive psychology, occupational health psychology, and sport psychology. It then synthesizes empirical work on stress, burnout, interpersonal relationships, and coping among coaches in order to identify the determinants and consequences of well-being in this profession. The chapter also points to the main gaps in the literature, in particular, how little empirical research addresses coaches specifically. It closes with recommendations for future research and for evidence-based interventions that can support sustainable psychological well-being among sports coaches.

items.title: Pursuing the good and human flourishing in professional life: virtue and ethics in the professions
items.abstract: Abstract An important question that vocational educators face is, namely, ‘How do we make people want to do good in professional life?’. This paper explores the concept of professionalism as an approach to ethics education – both in vocational degree programs and also in professional associations and colleges. I argue that current approaches to professionalism focused on guidelines or standards for good professional practice fall short of fostering intrinsic motivation among professionals to pursue the good in their work. I discuss how a framework of professionalism grounded in a robust sense of professional identity and virtue can fill the motivational gap that currently exists in some professionalism frameworks. I then explore how professionalism curriculums might go about fostering professional identity and virtue among students and junior professionals. The paper closes with a discussion of the advantages of integrating a robust professional identity and virtue framework into ethics education.

items.title: Push the Limits: Human‐Like Multimodal Extreme Embodied Intelligence for Autonomous Racing
items.abstract: Autonomous racing serves as a platform for testing embodied intelligence under extreme control conditions. It requires systems to operate at the limits of speed, actuation, and decision‐making. Inspired by human multimodality, which is the ability to integrate sensory inputs, learn adaptively, and transfer knowledge across domains for holistic situational awareness and optimal performance, we present Apex, an embodied intelligent agent that is implemented on an autonomous super‐formula racing vehicle on the Abu Dhabi Yas Marina F1 circuit. Apex integrates physics‐informed neural network‐enhanced perception, multimodal learning, and tasking capabilities to achieve high performance under extreme conditions. Leveraging real‐world data collected by a racing vehicle, Apex reduces lap times by 15% in time trials and achieves an 81% success rate in multivehicle attack‐defense scenarios, thus surpassing state‐of‐the‐art systems. This work not only underscores the transformative potential of multimodal embodied intelligence to master physical limits, but also addresses broader challenges in high‐performance robotic systems.

items.title: Questioning Instrumental Convergence in RLVR: Checkpoint Evidence from OLMo-3
items.abstract: Instrumental convergence is often invoked as a general reason to expect capable agents to acquire or express power-seeking subgoals: self-preservation, resource acquisition, deception, or resistance to oversight which poses an important threat to the society. For LLMs, reinforcement learning is the first stage of post-training that directly optimizes behavior against an objective; therefore, it is the stage where convergent instrumental behavior, on IC grounds, likely to appear. Does reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) make a model more likely to express instrumental-convergence behavior, or does this depend on the training regime, evaluation frame, and stage of post-training? We study this question as a checkpoint-conditioned behavioral trajectory rather than as a single before/after safety score. Using InstrumentalEval, we evaluate OLMo-3-7B-Think across SFT, DPO, 13 intermediate RLVR checkpoints, and the final RLVR model. The trajectory is nonmonotonic: instrumental rate rises from 25.0% at SFT to 46.1% near RLVR step 200, then falls to 11.8% at the final checkpoint. Paired item-level tests and step-wise regression support the final SFT-to-RLVR reduction. Prompt framing does not explain this pattern: a harmful-prompt indicator combined with other framing effects explains only 15% of within-checkpoint score variance on average, and Iterative Null-space Projection (INLP) removes a detectable framing direction without changing the SFT-to-final-RLVR gap. Together with preliminary 32B endpoint results (35.53% SFT to 22.37% RLVR final), these findings indicate that RLVR does not monotonically increase instrumental behavior in this setting: the rate rises early, then falls below the SFT baseline. The result is specific to this model family and benchmark, and judge agreement is moderate, so absolute rates should be read cautiously.

items.title: RAISE-STEM as a Translational Framework for Human-Centered AI Design in Higher Education Sociotechnical Learning Ecosystems
items.abstract: This chapter, per the authors, examines RAISE-STEM as a translational framework for human-centered artificial intelligence design in higher education. It responds to the gap between instrumental AI adoption and the broader sociotechnical challenges of agency, equity, data ethics, governance, and inclusive learning design. Drawing on sociotechnical theory, Actor-Network perspectives, and governance-oriented AI scholarship, the chapter reconceptualizes the five RAISE-STEM dimensions as mechanisms that connect classroom-level pedagogical change with institutional and ecosystem-level design. The chapter analyzes how macro, meso, and micro governance levels must operate coherently to support ethical, equitable, and pedagogically meaningful AI integration. It also introduces a Translational Design Architecture that maps each RAISE-STEM dimension to its human-centered design logic, governance level, key risk, and evaluation criterionwith a research agenda for participatory governance and empirical validation.

items.title: Reassessing Faith and Facts in AI-Augmented Modern Higher Education
items.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into modern higher education has produced a dual impact: while AI has opened new opportunities for innovation in teaching, learning, and research, it has also introduced significant challenges for academic practice. This paper explores how AI reshapes epistemic boundaries by challenging traditional notions and examines how confidence in institutional traditions and technological promise intersects with empirical data and algorithmic reasoning, and the ethical implications for transparent decision-making frameworks. By combining theoretical perspectives with practical examples, this paper highlights how AI is redefining epistemological foundations by the need to strengthen the relationship between faith and facts. The paper argues for a human-centred approach that promotes adaptive learning cultures. It concludes by proposing a forward-looking framework to help modern universities remain grounded in an AI-intensive future.

items.title: Reconstructing Digital Sovereignty through State Resilience Legal Policy: Citizen Protection after the Cyberattack on Indonesia’s Temporary National Data Center
items.abstract: The development of information technology and Artificial Intelligence (AI) has shifted the paradigm of state resilience away from protection oriented toward territorial areas and toward the protection of a borderless digital space. This shift presents new challenges for the state in protecting its citizens, as reflected in the cyberattack on Indonesia's Temporary National Data Center (PDNS) in 2024. Although Indonesia already has various regulations concerning information technology, cybersecurity, and personal data protection, national legal policy has not yet been fully able to build an integrated framework to respond to digital threats in the AI era. This research aims to analyze the legal policy of state resilience in protecting citizens through a case study of the cyberattack on PDNS, and to reconstruct legal policy based on Digital Sovereignty as a paradigm for strengthening state resilience. This research uses the normative legal research method with statutory, conceptual, and case approaches. The results show that the national legal framework remains sectoral in nature and has not been able to comprehensively integrate cybersecurity governance, data protection, and the use of AI. Therefore, this research offers a reconstruction of legal policy based on Digital Sovereignty, which places control over data, digital infrastructure, cybersecurity, and AI governance as a new foundation for strengthening state resilience while guaranteeing the protection of citizens' constitutional rights in the era of digital transformation. The proposed model integrates data sovereignty, infrastructure resilience, AI accountability, supply chain security, and digital human capacity through preventive, adaptive, rights based governance mechanisms for public institutions.

items.title: Reduced-DSP 200G/λ low-voltage slow-light silicon modulator enabled by built-in EO equalizer
items.abstract: Abstract Multi-Tb/s optical interconnects for artificial intelligence data centers necessitate high-speed, energy-efficient, and compact transceivers. However, conventional silicon Mach-Zehnder modulators are fundamentally limited by low modulation efficiency and large physical dimensions that typically extend several millimeters, requiring high-swing drivers and power-intensive digital signal processing to achieve data rates exceeding 100 Gb/s per lane. Here we show a silicon photonic crystal waveguide slow-light modulator that overcomes the bandwidth-efficiency trade-off via a built-in electro-optic equalizer. By monolithically integrating optical delay lines and crossings within segmented slow-light phase shifters, we synthesized an on-chip feedforward response that extends the 3-dB bandwidth. The fabricated modulator with a small device length of 320 µm demonstrated 140-Gb/s on-off keying operation with an energy consumption of 26 fJ/bit using drive voltages compatible with fin field-effect transistor-based complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology. Furthermore, four-level pulse amplitude modulation achieved 180 Gb/s without digital signal processing and 200 Gb/s with a low-complexity 11-tap digital equalizer. By reducing reliance on power-dissipating electronics, this strategy provides a potential route toward future dense multi-Tb/s co-packaged optics for energy-constrained switching systems.

items.title: Reference-Anchored Multi-Dilution Electronic Tongue for Ayurvedic Dravya Identification
items.abstract: Ayurvedic Dravya identification is an important process in Ayurveda, as the correct identification of medicinal substances supports their appropriate use and quality assessment. However, identifying Ayurvedic Dravya based on sensory characteristics such as Rasa (taste) can be challenging because different substances may exhibit similar taste profiles, while their responses can vary with sample concentration, solvent composition and preparation conditions. Traditional sensory evaluation also depends on human perception and may introduce subjectivity. An electronic tongue (E-tongue), which uses an array of chemical sensors to generate measurable response patterns, offers a potential approach for objective and repeatable taste-related analysis. This paper proposes a Reference-Anchored Multi-Dilution Electronic Tongue framework for Ayurvedic Dravya identification. The proposed system evaluates each sample at multiple predefined dilution levels to obtain a more representative sensor-response fingerprint. The collected signals are preprocessed, normalised and compared with reference fingerprints stored in a database using a deterministic distancebased matching method. Unlike approaches that depend on artificial intelligence or machine-learning classification, the proposed framework focuses on reference-based comparison, controlled sample preparation, sensor calibration and predefined acceptance criteria. The system is designed to provide the closest reference match when the similarity criteria are satisfied and a “No Reliable Match” result when the evidence is insufficient. The paper also discusses key challenges, including sensor drift, variation in sample composition, solvent effects, dilution consistency and the need for laboratory reference validation. The proposed framework may support the development of a transparent and reproducible electronic-tongue system for Ayurvedic Dravya screening. Experimental validation with authenticated samples is required to establish its identification performance, repeatability and practical suitability.

items.title: ReflectPO: Reflection-Guided Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.abstract: With external tools, large language models (LLMs) can tackle complex tasks through sustained environmental interaction. LLM-based agents are therefore increasingly used to tackle complex long-horizon tasks in real-world environments. However, these tasks involve sequential, interdependent decisions and changes in environmental states. Early execution errors affect subsequent interaction histories and environmental states, and their effects accumulate along the decision chain. To address this challenge, we propose Reflection-Guided Policy Optimization (ReflectPO), a reinforcement learning framework for autonomous error recovery in long-horizon tasks. ReflectPO comprises two core components. The first is Reflection-Guided Sampling. We use branch differences and repeated visits in interaction trajectories to construct hints for error recovery. The second is Tree-Structured Credit Assignment. We organize sampled trajectories into trees and assign action-level credit using parent--child reward differences and recovery gains. Experiments over two long-horizon tool-use benchmarks show that ReflectPO outperforms multiple existing baselines in most domains. It also achieves the best overall performance on average. Further analyses show that ReflectPO effectively improves agents' ability to recognize their own deviations, recover from erroneous states, and continue making progress toward task completion.

items.title: Regulatory Transformation in Toxicology
items.abstract: Toxicology is undergoing a paradigm shift that is being fuelled by artificial intelligence (AI), New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), and changing international regulatory systems. The classical toxicological methods, which may be based on animal experiments and to which tedious experimental guidelines are usually applied, are taken up and are more than ever supplemented by AI-based predictive models, high-throughput screening, in vitro testing, and calculations, all of which come within the scope of NAMs. These innovations are more efficient, cost-effective, and ethical than the other innovations and offer more mechanically relevant and human-relevant data. At the same time, the international policies are changing the regulatory demands, with the authorities of the European Union, the United States, and the Asian countries becoming more accepting of NAMs, encouraging harmonization, and incorporating AI into the safety evaluation frameworks.

items.title: Relación entre factores ergonómicos y frecuencia de síntomas musculoesqueléticos en empleados administrativos del Gobierno Regional, Bluefields
items.abstract: Workplace ergonomics is a key component of occupational health, as it considers the interaction between the worker, job characteristics, and the physical environment. The aim of this study was to determine the relationship between ergonomic factors and the frequency of musculoskeletal symptoms among administrative employees of the Regional Government in Bluefields, SACCR, Nicaragua. A quantitative, observational, cross-sectional, and correlational study was conducted with a sample of 112 workers. A questionnaire was used to assess ergonomic factors and musculoskeletal symptoms, complemented by semi-structured observation of workstations and the physical work environment. Data were processed using IBM SPSS 26® software, employing descriptive statistics, Pearson's chi-square test, and Spearman's rho. Of the participants, 96 (85.7 %) reported musculoskeletal symptoms, with frequent and very frequent pain being the most common presentations. Unfavorable ergonomic conditions related to posture and the physical environment were identified. The frequency of musculoskeletal symptoms showed statistically significant associations with the perception of work postures (ρ = −0.359; p < 0.001), ambient noise (ρ = 0.283; p = 0.002), humidity (ρ = 0.235; p = 0.020), and ambient heat (ρ = 0.215; p = 0.023). The findings demonstrate that specific postural factors as well as those related to equipment and the physical work environment are associated with the frequency of musculoskeletal symptoms, underscoring the need to strengthen ergonomic interventions focused on workstation design, environmental conditions, and work organization.

items.title: Relationship Between Chatgpt And Google Gemini Use And Mathematics Learning Interest Among Fifth-Grade Students At Sdn Kebalen 05
items.abstract: The objective of this study was to investigate the relationship between the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI), represented by ChatGPT and Google Gemini, and students’ interest in learning mathematics among fifth-grade students at SDN Kebalen 05. This study was motivated by the increasing use of generative AI as a learning tool and the low level of students’ interest in mathematics. A quantitative approach with a correlational survey design was employed. The population consisted of all fifth-grade students at SDN Kebalen 05, and a saturated sampling technique was used. Data were collected primarily through questionnaires, with observations, documentation, and interviews serving as supporting data. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Pearson Product-Moment correlation analysis. The results showed a strong positive relationship between the use of generative AI, represented by ChatGPT and Google Gemini, and students’ interest in mathematics learning (r = 0.682, p < 0.001). This finding indicates that higher use of generative AI was associated with higher interest in mathematics learning among fifth-grade students. The findings suggest that the appropriate use of generative AI may provide teachers with complementary tools for creating more interactive mathematics learning experiences and may be considered in supporting students’ learning interest. The study provides practical implications for teachers in integrating AI-based learning tools appropriately as complementary resources in primary mathematics education.

items.title: Reliable AI-Assisted Decisions via Selective Auditing
items.abstract: We consider online monitoring of an AI system that produces a sequence of decisions. At each round, the system outputs a proposed decision together with a confidence score estimating the trustworthiness of the decision. The decision and confidence score need not be produced by the same model: for example, one agent may propose a decision, while a separate verifier agent evaluates it and outputs a correctness or safety score. Based on this information, we must decide whether to accept the AI decision automatically or consult an expert, such as a human auditor, who reviews the proposal and either accepts or corrects it. We formulate this task as an online constrained optimization problem in which the goal is to minimize the frequency of expert auditing while guaranteeing that the fraction of AI errors that go unaudited stays below a user-defined threshold. We derive a family of algorithms with provable error-control guarantees with no assumptions, including a method that is optimally efficient: it asymptotically attains the best achievable auditing rate for both adversarial and i.i.d. data streams. Experiments on screening harmful requests to large language models, qualitative text annotation, and data labeling show that our methods achieve valid error control in practice while substantially reducing the need for human auditing compared to baselines.

items.title: Reported Transparency Practices in AI Use Among Journalism Professionals in Ecuador: Ethics, Self-Regulation, and Professional Challenges
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly incorporated into journalistic work, raising questions concerning transparency, authorship, editorial responsibility, human verification, and organizational governance. This study examines reported transparency practices and professional perceptions concerning AI use among journalism professionals linked to media organizations and news-production environments in Ecuador. A mixed-methods design combined a non-probability online survey of 53 eligible professionals with seven semi-structured interviews involving six journalism professionals and one communication academic with professional experience in journalism. The quantitative component was analyzed descriptively, while the qualitative component was examined through a deductive and interpretive analysis structured around four predefined thematic domains. AI use was reported by 48 of the 53 survey participants (90.6%), with both instrumental and generative applications identified. Among applicable responses, 39.5% reported the existence of a specific AI-related deontological code, 59.2% reported having received instructions from superiors, and 29.3% reported an obligation to disclose AI use to audiences. Human verification was the most frequently selected component of proposed internal AI rules (79.2%). The interviews showed uneven levels of organizational formalization, including verbal instructions, emerging guidelines, and differing thresholds for disclosure, while consistently emphasizing human editorial judgment and responsibility. The findings indicate that transparency in AI-assisted journalism is multidimensional and unevenly institutionalized across the professional environments represented in the study. These results provide sample-bound evidence from Ecuador and should not be interpreted as a national estimate of media transparency.

items.title: Research on Generative AI-Empowered Formative Assessment of Maritime English: Evaluation Indicators and Practical Paths
items.abstract: The Manila Amendments to the STCW Convention set compliance requirements for seafarers’ maritime communicative competence; however, higher-vocational Maritime English assessment still relies mainly on summative final-term evaluation, with high oral-assessment costs and delayed feedback. Drawing on the Outcomes-Based Education (OBE) philosophy and formative assessment theory, and supported by generative AI and intelligent speech-judgment technology, this study constructs a three-dimensional evaluation indicator system and designs a human-AI collaborative assessment closed loop of “pre-class diagnosis, in-class dynamic monitoring, and post-class iterative feedback”. A 16-week quasi-experiment shows that this model significantly improves students’ maritime English communicative competence, with the largest gain in the oral dimension (18.7% improvement in the experimental class versus 5.3% in the control class), and enhances students’ learning initiative. The study also analyzes the validity defects and academic-integrity risks of AI-driven assessment and proposes human-AI collaborative verification mechanisms, providing practical references for curriculum assessment reform of higher-vocational Maritime English and for STCW-aligned talent training.

items.title: Research Progress on AI-Driven Biomarker Prediction in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
items.abstract: This study overviews the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in the prediction of biomarkers for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Different from recent reviews on AI-driven radiogenomics that adopt clinical or imaging-based classification, this work innovatively takes AI model architecture as the core classification framework. By analyzing multimodal data (mainly CT) and modeling paradigms (radiomics, deep learning and fusion models), it reveals the current research status centered on EGFR mutation prediction. In terms of technological evolution, prediction models are evolving from traditional radiomics to end-to-end learning, Transformer architecture and multimodal perception-driven deep learning paradigms. This study deeply analyzes the performance differences among different models, fills the application gaps in existing reviews, and provides an important benchmark reference for the clinical optimization of AI-assisted tools and the promotion of standardized precise diagnosis and treatment of NSCLC.

items.title: Rethinking the Development Paradigm in Higher Education: Educational Communication in the Age of Technological Transformation
items.abstract: Abstract. This article critically re-examines the educational “development paradigm” as a foundational methodological assumption of higher education in the context of accelerating technological transformation and artificial intelligence. It is argued that the traditional understanding of development as an inherently positive educational objective requires critical reconsideration. It is demonstrated that human development, technological development, and educational development no longer represent convergent trajectories and therefore should be conceptualised as complementary yet analytically distinct dimensions. Based on theoretical analysis, comparative interpretation, and critical synthesis of interdisciplinary scholarship, the growing divergence between the exponential dynamics of technological innovation and the cognitive, ethical, and communicative capacities of human beings is examined. Particular attention is devoted to educational communication as the principal mechanism through which knowledge is co-constructed, meanings are negotiated, and human agency is sustained within technology-mediated learning environments. The concepts of sustainable development, limits to growth, limits of destruction, posthumanism, and technological singularity are analysed in relation to their implications for higher education. It is substantiated that technological innovation should be evaluated not solely in terms of efficiency and economic performance but also according to its contribution to human flourishing, ethical responsibility, and democratic participation. It is concluded that the educational “development paradigm” should be reconceptualised as a differentiated methodological framework integrating technological progress with human agency, communicative ecosystems, educational communication, and future-oriented education in an AI-mediated society. Keywords: higher education, educational “development paradigm”, pedagogical communication, AI-mediated communication, posthumanism, communicative ecosystems; future-oriented education.

items.title: Rethinking trust AI visibility in public services.
items.abstract: This article argues that trust in AI-mediated public services depends not only on whether systems are accurate, fair, or efficient, but on how their presence is made visible to the people affected by them. Across welfare, healthcare, and border governance, artificial intelligence increasingly shapes decisions about access, movement, support, and rights. Yet these systems often operate within familiar institutional procedures, making their role difficult to see, interpret, or challenge. The article develops the idea of AI visibility to explain how different forms of disclosure shape public trust. It distinguishes between invisible AI, partially visible AI, and fully disclosed AI, showing how each can produce different responses: misplaced confidence, confusion, suspicion, or informed challenge. By shifting attention from technical performance alone to the public experience of decision-making, the article shows that trust is shaped by whether people can understand where authority lies and how decisions are made. Foregrounding visibility helps reframe debates on algorithmic governance, institutional legitimacy, and accountability. In an increasingly automated state, the question is not only whether AI systems can be trusted, but whether their role in public decisions can be meaningfully seen. Working paper (Version 1.0). This manuscript has not yet undergone peer review.

items.title: Retrieval Is the New Record System: A Retrospective Analysis of Open-Source Contributions to Vector Databases and Embedding Infrastructure Underpinning Clinical AI (2025-2026)
items.abstract: Background. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) sits inside many clinical artificial intelligence (AI) prototypes. A language model answers from documents a retrieval layer selects first. If that layer returns the wrong documents, or returns nothing and reports success, the error starts before the model generates a word. Vector databases and embedding tools form that retrieval layer in most designs, so their defects count as health infrastructure defects. Purpose. This study analysed one contributor's public pull request (PR) record in vector database and retrieval projects. It asked three practical questions in sequence. What kinds of defects did the contributions address? What share of the work reached merge? Where did the process break down? Methods. On 21 October 2026 I extracted my full PR record through the GitHub API (author:rtmalikian): 213 PRs across 94 repositories (85 external projects and 9 of the author's own repositories). I defined a subset for vector databases and retrieval infrastructure: 39 PRs across 8 repositories. I coded each PR by status at extraction and read the review threads of seven cases in depth. Two cases from projects next to the subset, cocoindex-io/cocoindex and sentence-transformers, were read for comparison and kept out of the subset counts. Results. Of the 39 subset PRs, 13 merged, 18 were still open, and 8 closed unmerged. Among the 21 resolved PRs, 61.9% merged. Open PRs made up 46% of the subset, the highest share in any part of my record. The merged work clustered around one defect class: silent failure. Code accepted values it should have rejected, dropped errors in background threads, or hid missing data behind a normal response. The hardest case was a long-lived branch. pymilvus #3621 sat open from 20 June 2026 with 12 comments, merge conflicts, and a Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) gap on a sync commit. Conclusions. The code in this subset was rarely the slow part. Review time was. The fixes that landed shared one pattern: they made a system fail loudly, with an accurate message, at the point where bad data entered. A retrieval system that says "no record found" when it means "the index is corrupt" will mislead a clinician the way a silent defect misleads a developer.

items.title: REVIEW OF GENERATIVE AI AND CHATGPT:
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) has developed rapidly, enabling systems to produce text, images, code, audio, video, and other digital content. ChatGPT is a widely known conversational AI system that allows users to interact with large language models through natural-language prompts. This review paper synthesizes three published survey studies: Nah et al. on applications, challenges, and AI–human collaboration; Cong-Lem, Soyoof, and Tsering on the limitations and associated opportunities of ChatGPT; and Cao et al. on the development of AI-generated content (AIGC), from generative adversarial networks (GANs) to ChatGPT. The papers are compared across their objectives, scope, reported benefits, limitations, and future research directions. Across the studies, common opportunities include learning support, content creation, workflow assistance, and more accessible interaction with digital systems. Important concerns include inaccurate or fabricated outputs, bias, privacy and copyright issues, limited transparency, and excessive dependence on AI-generated responses. The review argues that responsible use requires human verification, privacy-aware practices, clear institutional guidance, and continued evaluation of AI systems. Rather than presenting new experimental results, this paper provides a comparative synthesis of the three selected studies and identifies areas that require further research. Keywords: Generative AI, ChatGPT, AI-generated content, AIGC, large language models, AI–human collaboration, limitations, responsible AI
